rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~91% 25bp / ~9% 50bp (CME FedWatch via Hercules, Nov 19 close); ECB Dec ~90%; BoE Dec ~80%; BoJ Dec ~84%; BoC Dec ~44%; RBA 4.85%, hold expected
rows.read: Markets still treat a December Fed hike as close to certain, and a sharp fall in US stocks has not changed that so far. The European Central Bank, Bank of England and Bank of Japan are also expected to hike, while Australian job losses suggest the Reserve Bank of Australia has peaked. US rates still look set to rise fastest, which keeps favouring the dollar.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: UK retail sales Oct +0.7% m/m (fcst 0.0%), +2.3% y/y; US claims 203K, Philly Fed 6.3, LEI −0.3%; Australia jobs Oct −43.5K, unemployment 4.9%
rows.read: UK shoppers spent more than expected in October, though much of it was stockpiling food, so it may not last. Soft US reports this week and Australia's job losses point to cooling elsewhere. The US still looks firmer than most, which keeps the dollar's lead intact for now.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Japan core CPI Oct 2.2% (fcst 2.3%), headline 2.3% (fcst 2.5%); Philly Fed prices paid 58.2; UK CPI Oct 3.6%; euro-area CPI Oct 4.0%
rows.read: Inflation is still above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Japan's inflation came in a touch below forecast but stayed above the Bank of Japan's goal, so a December hike there still looks likely. In the US, war-driven costs are still feeding through, which is why the Fed is slow to treat softer growth as a reason to stop.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: S&P 500 −2.0%, Nasdaq −2.3%, VIX ~28 (+16%) on Nov 19 (Journal Arta); USD/JPY −0.34%, USD/CHF −0.25% in Asia (Hercules)
rows.read: US stocks fell about 2% on Thursday, led by tech shares, and the market's fear gauge jumped. Money moved into the dollar, yen and franc, while the Aussie and kiwi lagged. Metals were sold to cover losses, so gold fell instead of rising.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Gold ~$3,552 (COMEX Dec), −3.2%; Brent Feb ~$92.6 (+0.7%), WTI Dec ~$83.4 (Hercules, Reuters; indicative)
rows.read: Gold fell more than 3% overnight to its lowest in about 14 months, which weighs on the Aussie. Oil edged up after Houthi strikes on Riyadh but is still heading for a third weekly fall, so the Canadian dollar gets little help. Cheaper oil this month still helps importers like the euro area and Japan.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC report of Nov 10 (out late after Veterans Day): hedge funds for USD, GBP, AUD and gold; against EUR, NZD, CAD and CHF; slightly against JPY; real money disagrees on EUR, GBP and AUD
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: ECB FSR: France debt 119% of GDP, deficit 5.5%; US October deficit $404B, a record for the month; US 10-year ~5.03% (Asia, Nov 20)
rows.read: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which weighs a little on trust in the dollar.
